# 1 Enoch Chapter 13 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Ge'ez MS; cf. 4QEn (Aramaic) | **Section:** Book of the Watchers

---

**1** Enoch went to Azazel and said: "Azazel, you will have no peace. A harsh sentence has been issued against you — you will be put in chains.

**2** You will receive no mercy and no answer to any request, because of the wickedness you taught and because of every act of godlessness, sin, and wrongdoing you introduced to humanity."

**3** Then I went and addressed all the Watchers together. They were terrified — fear and trembling gripped every one of them.

**4** They begged me to write a petition for them, asking for forgiveness, and to bring it before the Lord of heaven on their behalf.

**5** They could no longer speak to God directly, and they could not even raise their eyes toward heaven, because they were so ashamed of the sins that had brought judgment upon them.

**6** So I wrote out their petition — a prayer on behalf of each one of them, covering their individual deeds and their desire for forgiveness and long life.

**7** Then I went and sat down by the waters of Dan, in the region of Dan, south-southwest of Mount Hermon. I read their petition aloud until I fell asleep.

**8** As I slept, a dream came to me and visions poured down over me. I saw visions of judgment. Then a voice commanded me to go to the sons of heaven and deliver a verdict to them.

**9** When I woke up, I went back to the Watchers. I found them all gathered together, weeping, at Abel-mayin, between Lebanon and Senir, with their faces hidden.

**10** I told them everything I had seen in the dream, and I began to deliver the words of righteousness — pronouncing judgment on the Watchers of heaven.

---

*PNEUMA notes: Chapter 13 is rich in dramatic irony: the fallen angels who corrupted humanity must petition a human being to speak to God for them. Enoch's withdrawal to the waters of Dan (near Mt. Hermon, where the Watchers descended) and the dream-vision he receives there is the pivot point of the section. The dynamic rendering preserves the pathos of the Watchers' shame (v. 5) and the solemnity of Enoch's commission.*
